name: Beth Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes out with your name on it. I'll describe five pictures of the future and ask what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Harlow's, the family-run supermarket on the market square, eight till four most days. It's not huge, four tills, a bakery corner and a little butcher's counter. I do the tills, fill shelves, and on Fridays I help Mrs Harlow with the flower buckets out front. I'm still slow when the card machine plays up and I have to call Mr Harlow over, which I hate doing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the Harlows know everyone's name, including mine, and they pay better than the big chains to keep good staff. Outside work it's church on Sundays and planning the wedding, Mark and I are getting married next spring. Mark's an apprentice joiner. I live in my late gran's cottage, which she left me, so no rent, and I've put away over a year's worth of wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, things like that usually come to less than people say. At church I'd say people are still people. I don't go online much, I don't use any of that AI stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means Harlow's carries on, and I carry on. The only thing that ever worried me was the big chains opening out at the bypass, not robots. That worry doesn't go away just because AI fizzles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and try to get better with the card machine so I'm not calling Mr Harlow every day. We'd go ahead with the wedding as planned. I'd keep saving for when we have children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. It's how I'd like things to stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the big chains at the bypass. Does that worry you more than AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, honestly. When the discount place opened, Saturday takings at Harlow's dropped, and Mrs Harlow cut the Sunday hours. Harlow's could lose a lot of people to the bypass if prices keep going up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the wedding look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Chapel on the hill, then the village hall, with my aunt doing the food. Nothing fancy. We've saved for it already, so there's no borrowing.

say: I'd say things usually come to **less than people say**.
At church I'd say **people are still people**, AI or not.
think: **Harlow's carries on**, and so do I.
My real worry is the **big chains** at the bypass, not robots.
do: Get better with the **card machine** so I stop calling Mr Harlow.
Go ahead with the **wedding** next spring as planned.
Keep **saving** for when we have children.
S0.quote: The only thing that ever worried me was the big chains opening out at the bypass, not robots.
fieldNote: Her real threat is **chain competition**, which predates AI.
She lives rent-free in her **gran's cottage**, giving deep security.
Church and the **wedding** anchor her plans.

steps.text: Practise the card machine routine until it's second nature
Marry Mark at the chapel next spring as planned
Keep saving monthly for future children

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say The family shop where I work will be fine because people like being served by a person. I'd say the big chains can have their machines. At church I'd say we should look after each other through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots come slowly here, and Harlow's would be one of the last shops to buy them. But the chains would get cheaper with AI ordering and robots, and pull more customers away from the square. So my job's safe in one way and at risk in another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and maybe offer to help Mr Harlow with the bakery corner, since that's something the chains can't do the same. I'd save a bit more. I'd make sure our wedding stays small and paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for this year, but you feel it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try any AI tools if Harlow's brought them in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Harlow asked me to, I would, but I'd hate it. I'm not good with new things. I'd ask my brother to sit with me and show me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if Harlow's struggled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the Harlows, they've done everything right. I'd blame the big chains, and people who choose cheap over local. That's their right, but it has a cost.

say: I'd say people like being **served by a person**.
At church I'd say we should **look after each other** through it.
think: **Harlow's** would be one of the last shops to buy robots.
Cheaper **chains** would pull customers away from the square.
do: Offer to help with the **bakery corner**, which chains can't copy.
Keep the **wedding small** and fully paid.
S1.quote: The family shop where I work will be fine because people like being served by a person.
fieldNote: She sees the threat as **indirect**: cheaper chains, not her own till.
She'd use AI only if her **employer asked**.
She blames **chains and shoppers**, not the Harlows.

steps.text: Offer Mr Harlow help running the bakery corner
Raise the monthly savings a little
Keep the wedding small and paid in cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and I'd say we need to stick together, family and church. I don't believe in waiting for government to fix it. People need to work, not be paid to sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Harlow's can't last past 2031 if the chains have robots and AI that cheap. Even if the Harlows keep me, there might be no Harlow's. I don't know how to do anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every penny I could and put off having children for a while, which breaks my heart. I'd ask Mark if I could help in his joinery firm, sanding and finishing. I'd also ask the minister if the church needs help with anything paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I lie awake picturing the market square with the shutters down. It feels like the end of something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You have a cottage and over a year saved. Does that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, we won't be on the street. But money runs out, and I want to work. Sitting at home isn't how I was raised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mrs Harlow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mrs Harlow that whatever happens, I'll help until the last day. She took me on when nobody else would. You don't leave people like that.

say: I'd say we need to stick together through **family and church**.
I'd say people need **to work**, not be paid to sit at home.
think: **Harlow's** can't last past 2031 against cheap robot-run chains.
Even if the Harlows keep me, I **don't know** how to do anything else.
do: Put off having **children** for a while.
Ask Mark about helping in his **joinery** firm.
feel: **Frightened**, lying awake picturing the square with **shutters down**.
S2.quote: I lie awake picturing the market square with the shutters down.
fieldNote: She expects **Harlow's to close** and has no other skill.
Her values push her toward **family and church**, not government help.
Delaying **children** is the decision that hurts her most.

steps.text: Save every spare penny into the joint account
Delay starting a family for a couple of years
Help in Mark's joinery workshop, sanding and finishing
Ask the chapel minister about paid church work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to prepare as families and communities. I'd say young people should learn proper trades. At church we'd talk about it a lot, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means Harlow's probably keeps going till around 2034, maybe longer, they're stubborn. I'd want to have children before then. After that I'd want to be home with them, or working with Mark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a family sooner, while the job is steady, and keep saving. I'd learn some basic joinery from Mark at weekends, slowly, because I'm slow with new things. I'd keep working at Harlow's as long as they'll have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit. Less than the fast one, but it's still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you'd delay children. Now you'd have them sooner. Why the change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I'd rather have them while the job is still there and things are normal. In the fast one, everything is too uncertain. It's about having a calm few years to start a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think of moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Everyone I love is in this town. I'd rather be poorer here than better off somewhere I don't know anyone.

say: I'd say five years gives **families and communities** time to prepare.
I'd tell young people to learn **proper trades**.
think: Harlow's probably keeps going till around **2034**, maybe longer.
I'd want **children** before then, then be home or with Mark.
do: Start a **family sooner** while the job is steady.
Learn **basic joinery** from Mark at weekends.
Keep working at **Harlow's** as long as possible.
feel: **Anxious**, less than the fast one, but **still there**.
S3.quote: I'd rather be poorer here than better off somewhere I don't know anyone.
fieldNote: Five years **reverses** her family plan: children sooner, not later.
She would **not move**, valuing community over money.
Joinery with Mark is a **slow, familiar** backup.

steps.text: Try for a first child within the next two years
Learn basic joinery from Mark on Saturdays
Stay on at Harlow's as long as the shop lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and we'll manage like our grandparents did. I'd tell people not to panic. I'd say trades and family are what last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'll likely have children and be mostly home with them by the time the robots come in 2039. Mark's joinery has a good run too. So it might not touch me as much as I'd fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Harlow's, have the wedding, and start a family in a couple of years. I'd keep saving and maybe pay off any work on the cottage. I wouldn't do anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly settled. It feels far enough away to live normally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Mark's joinery is hit by robots later, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd have the cottage, savings and each other. We'd find a way, people always have. But I'd rather not think that far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the long version that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The town. Even if my fiancé Mark and I are fine, the market square might empty out. I'd miss Harlow's more than the job itself.

say: I'd say we'll manage like our **grandparents** did.
I'd tell people not to panic, because **trades and family** are what last.
think: I'll likely be **home with children** by the time robots arrive.
Mark's **joinery** has a good run too.
do: Carry on at **Harlow's** and have the wedding.
Start a **family** in a couple of years.
Keep **saving** and fix up the cottage.
S4.quote: Even if my fiancé Mark and I are fine, the market square might empty out.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **traditional plan** play out mostly untouched.
Her remaining worry is the **town square**, not her income.
She plans **nothing new** and trusts savings and family.

steps.text: Carry on working at Harlow's after the wedding
Start a family in about two years
Save for repairs to the cottage roof

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time for Harlow's or for me. What would help is people choosing to shop local, and apprenticeships for grown-ups, so you can learn a trade without going back to school. Help from family and church matters more than government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. It's what gets people like me through the frightening bits. I'd be a lot more scared about robots without church on Sunday mornings.

headlineQuote: I'd be a lot more scared about robots without church on Sunday mornings.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old** cashier at a small family-run supermarket on a market square.
She lives rent-free in her **late gran's cottage** and has over a year of wages saved.
She's marrying Mark, an apprentice joiner, and **faith and family** shape her choices.
She's calm in AI Plateau but **alarmed** by AGI by 2028, picturing the square shut.
She never uses AI and would **change little**, leaning on family, church and joinery with Mark.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time for Harlow's or for her to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: **Adult apprenticeships** so she can learn a trade without school.
